issues.legal_issue: Occupants who reside with a tenant as paying guests, under arrangements that leave the premises in the tenant’s occupation and give them no independent interest in the premises, are not sub-tenants on those facts.
material_facts: The tenant produced agreements stating that the occupants would reside with him as paying guests and that their payments included food.
The agreements stated that the premises would remain in the tenant’s occupation.
The trial court and first appellate court found that the occupants were paying guests and that no part of the premises had been sub-let.
issues.conclusion: The occupants were paying guests, not sub-tenants, so the eviction decree on the ground of unauthorized subletting could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(a) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act permits eviction on the ground of unauthorized subletting. The agreements here created no interest in any part of the premises in favour of the paying guests. The Court expressed no definite opinion on whether exclusive possession raises a burden on the tenant to show that the occupant is not a sub-tenant.

predicates.eviction_proceeding_for_subletting: A landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had sub-let part of the premises without consent.
predicates.occupants_stayed_as_paying_guests_with_t: The other occupants resided with the tenant as paying guests, with their payments covering services such as food.
predicates.tenant_retained_occupation: The tenant continued to occupy the premises along with the other occupants.
predicates.agreements_created_no_independent_intere: The agreements provided that the occupants would live as guests and would receive no independent interest in any part of the premises.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding alleges unauthorized subletting, and the occupants stayed as paying guests with the tenant, the tenant retained occupation, and the agreements created no independent interest, eviction for unauthorized subletting is not allowed.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a second appeal cannot interfere with concurrent factual findings of the trial court and first appellate court when those findings are not perverse.
material_facts: The trial court found that the occupants were not sub-tenants and that the tenant had not sub-let any part of the premises.
The first appellate court upheld those findings.
The High Court disturbed the concurrent findings, although the Supreme Court considered them correct and not perverse.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not interfere with the concurrent findings in second appeal, and its eviction decree on the subletting ground had to be set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that concurrent findings of fact cannot be interfered with by a High Court in second appeal where the findings are not perverse. No earlier case or specific statutory provision was cited for this principle.

predicates.second_appeal_from_concurrent_factual_fi: The matter is a second appeal challenging factual findings made by the trial court and upheld by the first appellate court.
predicates.findings_are_not_perverse: The concurrent factual findings are supported by the evidence and are not perverse.

issues.definition: In a second appeal from concurrent factual findings, if those findings are not perverse, they are not interfered with.

issues.legal_issue: A new ground for eviction that was not pleaded or raised in the trial court or first appeal cannot be introduced for the first time in a second appeal.
material_facts: The landlord had not pleaded the change-of-purpose ground in the plaint.
No issue on that ground was framed, and the ground was not urged before either the trial court or the first appellate court.
The landlord raised the ground for the first time in the High Court in second appeal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have entertained the new eviction ground in the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that raising this ground for the first time in second appeal was impermissible where it had not been pleaded, made the subject of an issue, or urged in the lower courts. No specific statutory provision or earlier case was cited for this procedural conclusion.

rule.if: second_appeal_in_eviction_proceeding and ground_absent_from_pleadings and no_issue_on_ground and ground_not_raised_in_lower_courts

predicates.second_appeal_in_eviction_proceeding: The matter is a second appeal in an eviction proceeding.
predicates.ground_absent_from_pleadings: The party seeking eviction did not include the ground in the initiating pleading.
predicates.no_issue_on_ground: The lower court did not frame an issue on that ground.
predicates.ground_not_raised_in_lower_courts: The party did not urge that ground before the trial court or first appellate court.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding on second appeal, a ground absent from the pleadings, not made the subject of an issue, and not raised in the lower courts is not entertained.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant does not use residential premises for a different purpose merely by taking paying guests into a spare room while continuing to reside there with family and using the premises residentially.
material_facts: The premises were let for residential use.
The tenant continued to reside there with family members.
The tenant took one or two paying guests at a time into a spare room and charged an amount that included food.
The tenant did not carry on a business in the premises, which continued to be used for residential purposes by the tenant, family, and guests.
issues.conclusion: The premises continued to be used for a residential purpose, so the eviction decree on the different-purpose ground could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(h) of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act provides a ground for eviction where premises are used for a purpose different from the purpose for which they were let. On these facts, taking paying guests while continuing residential occupation did not change the purpose of use.

rule.if: eviction_proceeding_for_different_use and premises_let_for_residential_use and tenant_and_family_continued_residing and paying_guests_stayed_in_spare_room and no_business_carried_on

predicates.eviction_proceeding_for_different_use: A landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant used the premises for a purpose different from the letting purpose.
predicates.premises_let_for_residential_use: The premises were let to the tenant for residential use.
predicates.tenant_and_family_continued_residing: The tenant continued to live in the premises with family members.
predicates.paying_guests_stayed_in_spare_room: The tenant accommodated paying guests in a spare room while continuing to occupy the premises.
predicates.no_business_carried_on: The tenant did not conduct a business in the premises.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding alleging different use, if the premises were let for residential use, the tenant and family continued to reside there, paying guests stayed in a spare room, and no business was carried on, the residential purpose is not treated as changed.
